source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Search over thoughts beat plain prompting on Game of 24 with GPT-4. Breadth 1 already helped a lot; breadth 5 helped more.
numbers: Game of 24, 100 games, GPT-4 success: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC k=100 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Oracle best-of-100: IO 33%, CoT 49%.
limits: One task family with clean states and a checkable end. The strongest baseline is oracle best-of-100, not a cost-matched vote. Authors used task-specific decomposition.
agent_relevance: Gain comes from stepwise state expansion plus pruning, which a coded controller can do. Compare against compute-matched voting before adopting.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, Table 2 and Appendix B.3 cost analysis
finding: ToT costs about as much as 100 CoT samples, and still wins on Game of 24. On Creative Writing it costs about 5 times IO or CoT.
numbers: Game of 24 per case: IO best-of-100 $0.13 (33%), CoT best-of-100 $0.47 (49%), ToT $0.74 (74%). ToT 5.5k completion tokens vs CoT-100 6.7k. Creative Writing ToT 4k/2.9k tokens vs 0.9k/0.4k for IO or CoT.
limits: GPT-4 prices of 2023. Cost parity is only with 100 samples, which few users run.
agent_relevance: Search is a compute purchase. Budget it in code and spend it only where a check can prune.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, ablation on Mini Crosswords (Table 3)
finding: On crosswords, removing pruning or backtracking cut results sharply. Backtracking mattered most for whole-game success.
numbers: 156 games scraped; test on 20. Word-level success: IO/CoT under 16%, ToT 60%, solved 4 of 20 games. Ablation letter success: ToT 78, +best state 82.4, -prune 65.4, -backtrack 54.6. Game-level: ToT 20%, -prune 5%, -backtrack 5%.
limits: 20 test games only. Search steps capped at 100. Specialized NLP pipelines solve crosswords far better.
agent_relevance: Supports a state with a dead-end detector and a return-to-parent move (backtracking) triggered by a failed check, not by schedule.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, generation vs evaluation split with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4
finding: Weaker model lost most gain. Swapping which model generates or evaluates showed that generating good candidate thoughts was the bottleneck on Game of 24.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-3.5 ToT 19% vs GPT-4 ToT 74%. GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%. GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%. Creative Writing: ToT > CoT > IO held for GPT-3.5.
limits: Single task for the split. Prompt had to change to 3-shot proposals to work for GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Operator quality (candidate generation) matters more than evaluator quality in this task. Do not assume a cheap judge is the weak link.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: The LLM as its own world model plus Monte Carlo tree search solved Blocksworld far better than CoT, and gains grew with plan length. Beat GPT-4 CoT with a 33B model.
numbers: Blocksworld success, LLaMA-33B: CoT 2-step 0.17, 4-step 0.02, 6-step 0.00; RAP(20) 1.00, 0.88, 0.42. GPT-4 CoT 0.50, 0.63, 0.40. Llama-2 70B full set Easy all: CoT 0.08, RAP(10) 0.65. Hard all: CoT 0.05, RAP(10) 0.51.
limits: RAP uses task-specific reward terms. Reward for step t sees only the current state, which makes late steps easier (authors say so). 10 to 20 iterations per problem.
agent_relevance: Explicit state tracking after each action prevents illegal moves. Supports a coded state that the model must update and the program can check.

source: Hao et al. (2023) RAP, math and logic results and reward ablation
finding: On GSM8k and ProntoQA the gain over strong baselines is small. Reward choice mattered: action likelihood plus task reward beat single rewards; likelihood reward hurt GSM8k with more iterations.
numbers: GSM8k: CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, RAP(1) 48.6, RAP(10) 51.6 (aggregate version higher). ProntoQA prediction 94.2 vs CoT 87.8; proof accuracy 78.8 vs 64.8.
limits: GSM8k RAP vs CoT+SC(10) differs by only a few points. Ablation on first 300 GSM8k items only. LLaMA-33B base.
agent_relevance: Where a vote is already strong, tree search adds little. The extra part that helps is a self-evaluation signal, which G1 and G5 treat with care.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: MCTS with environment feedback and reflection beat ToT, RAP and Reflexion on code, QA and web tasks. Gains depend on external feedback.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 GPT-3.5: CoT 46.9, ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. GPT-4: base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7. WebShop table text garbled in PDF extraction; not recorded. Game of 24 GPT-3.5: CoT .08, Reflexion .12, ToT .20, RAP .40, LATS .44.
limits: Needs ability to revert environment state. Higher cost than ReAct. HumanEval uses generated tests as feedback. Authors report own re-runs of baselines.
agent_relevance: The big win is real test output feeding the value, in line with G2 and G3. The tree adds a little on top of the feedback.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) LATS ablations and cost on HotPotQA
finding: Ablations show which parts carry the gain. Removing the LM value heuristic hurt most; removing reflection hurt a little; DFS instead of MCTS hurt. LATS used fewer nodes than ToT or RAP at equal sample count.
numbers: HotPotQA EM: LATS 0.63; no reflection 0.58; DFS 0.42; no LM heuristic 0.37; ToT(ReAct) 0.39; RAP(ReAct) 0.54. Nodes to success at k=50: ToT 84.05, RAP 70.60, LATS 66.65 (accuracy .49, .54, .61).
limits: Failed trajectories not counted in node averages. n=5 children, k=50 trajectories, so about 250 model calls per question.
agent_relevance: The value function is the lever. Make it a coded check where possible.

source: Long (2023) Large Language Model Guided Tree-of-Thought
finding: A ToT controller with a rule-based Sudoku checker and backtrack memory outperformed zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot CoT on 3x3, 4x4, 5x5 Sudoku. It failed on some larger puzzles.
numbers: Ten puzzles per size. 3x3 ToT 100%. 4x4 ToT 9 of 10 solved. 5x5 ToT 8 of 10 solved. ToT success 80% higher than one-shot or few-shot on 4x4 and 60% higher on 5x5. Max 100 conversation rounds.
limits: Ten puzzles per set. Tiny sample, no confidence intervals. Rule-based controller does not know if a board can still be completed.
agent_relevance: A checker that detects rule violation lets the program backtrack. This is the G2 pattern in a search setting. Sample too small to rely on.

source: Salahi, Gurusankar, Edamadaka (2024) Stanford CS224N project: More Effectively Searching Trees of Thought
finding: Re-ran Game of 24 with open models. The gap between tree and chain nearly vanished once the value function was better. Choice of search algorithm (BFS vs MCTS) did not matter much.
numbers: Default Mixtral-8x7B value fn: BFS-1 18.18%, BFS-3 41.41%, BFS-5 66.66%. Finetuned Mistral-7B value fn: BFS-1 47.47%, BFS-5 63.63%. Oracle: BFS-1 32.32%, BFS-5 61.61%. Finetuned value fn gain at BFS-1 was 29.29 points. About 99 problems. Finetuned fn runtime 0.53s vs default 3.52s per call.
limits: Student project, not peer reviewed. Different models than ToT paper. About 99 test items, so one item is about 1 point.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: much of ToT gain is a better evaluator, not tree structure. Test evaluator quality before adding branching.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Autonomous LLM planning is poor. With an external sound verifier looping back, results rise a lot. With obfuscated predicate names the LLM stops helping.
numbers: Blocksworld, 600 instances, one-shot/zero-shot correct: GPT-4o 28.3%/35.5%, GPT-4-Turbo 23%/40.1%, Claude-3-Opus 48.1%/59.3%. Mystery BW: all models 0 to 2.5%. With VAL back-prompting up to 15 rounds: Blocks World 82%, Logistics 70%; Mystery BW about 10%. About 12% of GPT-4 plans were valid in earlier work.
limits: Position paper from a group that argues LLMs cannot plan. Blocksworld is a narrow domain. Numbers partly from earlier papers by same group.
agent_relevance: Strongest support for G2 and G3: a sound external verifier plus model proposals. Also shows the problem representation (names) changes the space the model can handle.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2022) PlanBench: An Extensible Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Planning and Reasoning about Change
finding: Introduced Blocksworld and Logistics test suites with simple auxiliary tasks and real plan generation. GPT-4 and InstructGPT3 did poorly on real planning in 2022.
numbers: Table 1 text garbled in PDF extraction. Paper states GPT-4 best on auxiliary goal reformulation tasks and falls short on most Blocksworld planning cases; exact percentages not recorded.
limits: Table layout garbled in PDF text; read figures with care. Early models. Static test set can only be an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Source of the standard planning test. The same group re-tests every new model, which gives a time series.

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
finding: A model trained for long reasoning (o1) greatly improved on Blocksworld but not to a reliable level. Gains drop with obfuscation, long plans and unsolvable goals. Accuracy comes at higher time and cost than a classical planner.
numbers: Blocksworld 600 instances: o1-preview 97.8%, o1-mini 56.6%. Mystery BW: 52.8% (o1-preview), 19.1% (o1-mini). Randomized Mystery BW: 37.3%. 110 larger problems (20 to 40 steps): o1-preview 23.63%. Unsolvable goals: only 27% correctly flagged on BW, 16% on randomized mystery. Fast Downward 100% in 0.265s vs o1-preview 40.43s average.
limits: o1 hidden trace, outputs needed GPT-4o-mini translation to PDDL. Preview model only. Same group as b11.
agent_relevance: Even a model trained to search internally degrades with longer horizons and relabelled representations. Keep external state and verification; also test with unsolvable instances.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: CoT gains in Blocksworld came only when the example algorithm matched the problem class very closely, and they fell as stacks grew past the example size. Self-consistency did not fix this.
numbers: Table-to-stack, 261 instances, GPT-4-Turbo/Claude-3-Opus/GPT-4: zero-shot 19.1/9.96/3.83%; zero-shot CoT 21/10.34/4.98%; Blocksworld universal algorithm 37.1/37.1/51.3%; stacking prompt 40.6/24.5/59.3%. Synthetic domains zero-shot vs manual CoT: CF 56.38 vs 98.89%, LLC 10.00 vs 51.06%, LVC 5.75 vs 27.00%.
limits: Few models, simple domains, one research group. Claims about learning algorithms from demonstrations are an interpretation.
agent_relevance: Operators written as generic instructions fail to generalize; narrow worked examples work but are costly. Fits our preference for code-run procedures over model-followed algorithms.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans? / Stechly et al. (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong (graph coloring)
finding: On graph coloring, GPT-4 self-critique made results worse. A sound external verifier improved them, but richer feedback added nothing over a bare no. Most of the gain came from extra tries.
numbers: 100 instances. No backprompt baseline 16%. Self-critique backprompt: 1 of 100 correct. Sound verifier: nearly 40%; binary vs full error list differences insignificant. Sampling n=15 at t=1.0 reached about 40%, same as backprompting.
limits: Graph coloring only. One model (GPT-4). Small set of 100.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2/G4: revision gains may be resampling in disguise. Control with matched sample budget.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, self-correction did not help and often hurt. With an oracle label to stop, it looked like a big gain, which explains earlier positive claims.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (round 1) -> 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, GPT-4 97.5.
limits: Prompts followed source papers; task type matters (plan, code tasks differ). 2023 models.
agent_relevance: The revision step in any search loop must be gated by a real signal (G2), or the loop makes accuracy worse.

source: Xu et al. (2024) LLMs and the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus: Successes, Failures, and the Importance of Object-based Representations (TMLR)
finding: Changing how the problem is written (text grid vs object graph) changed what GPT-4 could solve. Failure was loss of object cohesion in text. Object-based encoding nearly doubled solved tasks.
numbers: 50 easy ARC tasks: direct grid GPT-4 13 of 50; object-based encoding 23 of 50 (object JSON with CoT: 20 of 50 for GPT-4, 5 for GPT-3.5). Full ARC training set 81 of 400 with best text encoding. Mini-ARC 35 of 149. Of 13 solved, only 3 had correct reasoning.
limits: Object extraction came from a symbolic ARC solver (ARGA), so part of the gain is outsourced. Easy subset only.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for the Simon-and-Hayes idea in an LLM: the representation sets the state space. Operator O1 (restate) can matter more than extra search. Right answers were often reached with wrong reasoning.

source: Fansher, Shah, Helie (2022) The Effect of Mode of Presentation on Tower of Hanoi Problem Solving
finding: Human solvers finished Tower of Hanoi more often with an external display, but used fewer moves when working in their heads. External display speeds moves; internal representation promotes planning.
numbers: Experiment 1, final n=129 (3 excluded for rule misunderstanding, 11 for computer fault), at least 30 per condition. 4-disk completion: computer 100% vs mental 91%. 5-disk completion: computer 93% vs mental 63% (B=-2.67, p=.001). Time between moves higher in mental condition (t(75.99)=-5.62, p<.001). 15 min cap. Experiment 2 on Prolific replicated the pattern.
limits: Online sample, 15 min limit, mental condition used a static picture and spoken move reports. Transfer finding is moderate.
agent_relevance: External state helps success; internal planning helps efficiency. An agent with a written, code-held state should expect more reliable but less planned moves; consider forcing a lookahead step.

source: Jarusek and Pelanek (2011) What Determines Difficulty of Transport Puzzles? (FLAIRS)
finding: Solution length and state space size do not explain human difficulty well. A random-plus-greedy walk model of the state graph (dead ends, direction of moves) predicted solve times better for two of three puzzles.
numbers: Over 100 instances of Sokoban (35), Rush Hour (45), Replacement puzzle (40); hundreds of hours of data. Spearman with solve time: Rush Hour shortest path 0.90 vs model 0.90; Sokoban 0.41 vs 0.61; Replacement 0.21 vs 0.49. Pearson Sokoban 0.19 vs 0.39 (0.80 after removing one outlier). Best optimality bonus B about 25 in all three.
limits: Web-collected data, self-selected solvers. Model does not claim cognitive realism. Applies to puzzles with reversible or irreversible moves differently.
agent_relevance: Difficulty sits in the graph shape (dead ends, irreversible moves), not only the path length. Flag irreversible operators and dead-end regions in our state graph.

source: Kotovsky, Hayes, Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? Evidence from Tower of Hanoi
finding: Isomorphs of Tower of Hanoi that look alike in structure differ greatly in difficulty. Difficulty was tied to the size of the processing steps and to how well the rules could be kept in mind.
numbers: not opened; only the citation was confirmed (Cognitive Psychology 17, 248-294).
limits: Full text not read this session. Details come from secondary descriptions in b19 and a search summary. Treat as pointer only.
agent_relevance: Predicts that reformulating a task into a lower-load isomorph should help. Needs a full read before use.

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: Explorations in the problem space of difficulty
finding: Chinese ring puzzle study of why some problems stay hard even after learning. Cited by b19 as the second classic isomorph-difficulty result.
numbers: not opened; only the citation was confirmed (Cognitive Psychology 22, 143-183).
limits: Only bibliographic record seen.
agent_relevance: Follow up in a later pass; likely about problems where the right move increases distance from the goal.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (JEP:LMC 29(5), 1017)
finding: Rival theories of insight tested on one problem. Representational change (constraint relaxing, chunk decomposition) predicted performance better than progress monitoring, though both got some support. Eye movement data used.
numbers: No numbers on the repository page; abstract only.
limits: Abstract page only, not the full paper. Single problem type.
agent_relevance: Insight is a critique of plain state-space search: sometimes the representation itself must change. Supports reframing (O-restate) fired by an impasse signal, not by schedule (G1).

source: Oellinger, Jones, Faber, Knoblich (2013) as summarised in web search of eight-coin problem
finding: On the eight-coin problem, two sources of difficulty: the constraint that the solution lies in two dimensions, and the need to break perceptual groupings. Authors say both support representational change theory.
numbers: not opened; search summary only.
limits: Search snippet only. Not read.
agent_relevance: Adds a second case that a rep-change operator can be separated into two named moves: lift a constraint, split a chunk.

source: Search summary on impasse and insight (Jones 2003 context)
finding: Reaching an impasse does not by itself produce a representational change; sometimes the solver stays stuck.
numbers: none seen
limits: Secondary statement from a search summary, not a read source.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: an impasse detector tells you when to switch, not what to switch to. The switch needs its own generator and check.

source: Cross-source synthesis: where search helps and where it does not (b01, b05, b07, b10, b15)
finding: Across the opened papers, search gains are largest when (1) there is a checkable step state, (2) the checker is external or cheap and reliable, (3) baselines are weak chains. Gains shrink against a strong voting baseline or a good evaluator.
numbers: Large gain: Game of 24 4% to 74% (b01); Blocksworld 6-step 0.00 to 0.42 (b05). Small gain: GSM8k RAP(10) 51.6 vs CoT+SC(10) 46.8 (b06). Value-function swap closes the gap at BFS-1 by 29.29 points (b10). Resampling alone matches backprompt: 40% (b15).
limits: Author synthesis across different models, years and tasks; no single compute-matched study found in this pass.
agent_relevance: Rule for our schema: spend search budget only where code can check a step. Otherwise vote or resample. A compute-matched test on our own tasks is still missing.

source: Mirror paper search summary (arXiv 2402.14963) on majority voting in trees
finding: Summary says simple majority voting helps chain prompts but not over a generated tree, because bad expansions count as much as good ones.
numbers: not opened
limits: Seen through search snippet only. Not read.
agent_relevance: Weak pointer: voting across tree nodes needs weights from checks. Verify before relying.

source: Open problem list from opened sources: ill-defined problems and external-state critique
finding: All LLM search work above uses well-defined tasks with a known goal test (24, Blocksworld, Sudoku, crosswords, unit tests). The sources contain no measured gain on ill-defined problems with no goal test.
numbers: None; absence noted across b01, b05, b07, b09, b11.
limits: Absence of evidence in the papers read, not a systematic search for such studies.
agent_relevance: For our open-ended tasks, a state-space loop has no proven gain. Use it where a verifier exists; otherwise do not add search.

source: Open questions list for next pass
finding: Not yet read: Kotovsky 1985 full text with exact move times, Simon and Hayes 1976 isomorph effect sizes, Knoblich 2001 numbers, Zhang and Norman 1994, MacGregor 2001, a compute-matched ToT vs self-consistency study.
numbers: none
limits: Paywalled or not found in this pass.
agent_relevance: Fetch these before final synthesis of the subfield.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Plain repeated sampling is a strong baseline for any tree search when an automatic checker exists. Without a checker, picking the answer (vote, reward model) plateaus.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples (single-sample state of the art 43%). CodeContests, Gemma-2B: coverage 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000. MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote and reward models plateau near 100 samples.
limits: Coverage counts a problem solved if any sample is right, so it is an upper bound unless a verifier exists. Cost grows linearly with samples.
agent_relevance: Any search claim must beat matched-token sampling plus a real checker (G4, G5, G7). Selection, not generation, is the bottleneck without a checker.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic tasks
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 CoT papers plus own runs on 20 datasets and 14 models: step-by-step text helps mostly where a symbolic step is needed. A plan-then-tool-solver beats plan-then-CoT-solver.
numbers: Average CoT gain: math 14.2 points, symbolic 12.3, logical 6.9; all other categories 56.8 with CoT vs 56.1 without. On MMLU up to 95% of the gain is on questions whose answer or output contains an equals sign.
limits: Benchmarks differ in prompts; the symbolic label is the authors' own judgement.
agent_relevance: Spend thinking budget by problem class (S0 GATE). Use code, not text, for the symbolic execution part (section 1).

source: Koh et al. (2024/2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents (TMLR)
finding: Best-first search in the real environment with a model-judged value function raises web-agent success, and success rises with search budget.
numbers: VisualWebArena, GPT-4o: 18.9% to 26.4% (+39.7% relative). WebArena, GPT-4o: 15.0% to 19.2% (+28.0%). Llama-3-70B on VWA: 7.6% to 16.7% (+119.7%). 200-task VWA subset with budget c=20: 24.5% to 37.0% (+51.0%); depth d=5, branching b=5.
limits: Absolute success stays below 27%. Search can cost up to 20 times more model calls per step. The value function is itself a model judgement.
agent_relevance: G12 holds: gains scale with budget but so does cost. Small models gain most in relative terms (foothold needed).

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Gundawar, Kambhampati (2024) Planning in Strawberry Fields (o1 planning and scheduling, LRM-Modulo)
finding: A reasoning model plus an external verifier loop is the best system, and a cheap model in a verifier loop can match or beat a reasoning model for less money.
numbers: o1-preview with verifier loop: harder Blocksworld 98.2% within 7 iterations; graph coloring up to 94%; Sokoban 12.7% to 43.6%. Calendar scheduling: o1-mini costs $2.70 for 94%; GPT-4o-mini in a 50-iteration verifier loop costs $2.48 for 97%. Plain o1-preview on Blocksworld 97.8% but about 40 s per item vs 0.12 s for a classical planner.
limits: Authors argue LLMs cannot plan alone. Iterations capped at 10 for cost; trip planning stopped early because of rising cost.
agent_relevance: Supports G2, G5, G7: verifier loops buy accuracy per dollar. Report cost per solved item.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint Relaxation and Chunk Decomposition in Insight Problem Solving (JEP:LMC 25)
finding: Insight cast as repeated impasse in a wrong problem space. Difficulty tracked how wide a constraint had to be relaxed and how tight a chunk had to be broken, predicted in advance on matchstick arithmetic.
numbers: Exp 1A (N=20, 5-min limit): median solution time A 40 s, B 155 s, C 300 s (cap), D 140 s. Transfer to block 2 only for harder types (B p<.05, C p<.001, none for A). Exp 2 N=78. Exp 3 N=34: regular Type C 61% solved in block 1 vs all solved when tautological.
limits: One task family. Type B vs A not significant on frequency in one experiment (ceiling 96% vs 90%). Times capped. Wilcoxon tests, small samples.
agent_relevance: An impasse means the representation is wrong. Re-represent by relaxing one named constraint, only after a check fails (G1).

source: Schooler, Ohlsson, Brooks (1993) Thoughts beyond words (JEP:General 122); Gilhooly et al. (2010); Fleck and Weisberg (2004), all as summarised in Kiyokawa and Dienes (2019)
finding: Verbal overshadowing of insight (talking aloud hurts insight problems) is contested. One replication found a much smaller interaction; another found none.
numbers: Schooler Exp 3: verbalizing cut percent solved in 6 min by about 25% on insight problems and about 5% on non-insight (20-point interaction). Gilhooly raw interaction 4% (SE 3.1%) vs about 13% expected after time correction; Bayes factor 0.92, inconclusive. Fleck and Weisberg: no think-aloud effect on the candle problem. Kiyokawa and Dienes (35 participants): T-puzzle solved 3 of 11 toward-self, 5 of 12 toward-other, 8 of 11 control.
limits: Read through a later paper's summary, not the original. Small samples. Search summary also says a 2025 study found no solution-rate change.
agent_relevance: Do not build an agent rule on this effect. It is unproven, so forced explanation steps on insight-type items stay behind G1.

source: Fox, Ericsson, Best (2011) Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? (Psychological Bulletin 137)
finding: Search-summary only. Meta-analysis of the think-aloud method behind Newell and Simon's protocol analysis: pure think-aloud is not reactive on accuracy, but explaining or describing is.
numbers: 94 studies, nearly 3,500 participants; think-aloud effect r = -.03 (null); explanation-type reporting raised performance; all verbal reporting added time.
limits: Full text not opened; figures from a web-search summary.
agent_relevance: Protocol data are valid evidence about steps. An agent's written explanation is an intervention that changes the answer, not a neutral window (G10).
